en: An Outline of the Heart Sutra, composed by Li Zhuowu.
The Heart Sutra is the Buddha’s concise and essential path to the mind. The mind is fundamentally non-existent, yet worldly people delusively regard it as such.
There is existence, yet there is also no non-existence; yet the student clings to it as being non-existent. By dividing existence and non-existence, one establishes the subject and the object;
this is self-imposed entanglement, self-inflicted terror, and self-induced perversion. How could one then attain mastery? Do you not observe the Sovereign Bodhisattva alone?
His wisdom and practice are profound; he has already reached the further shore of mastery. At such a time—
Naturally, one perceives that the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are all empty. Fundamentally, there is no birth-and-death to be found;
thus, one is able to transcend the ocean of suffering of birth-and-death and deliver oneself from all miseries and calamities.

This is the essential summary of this sutra. The subsequent passages explain this point repeatedly and exhaustively to clarify it. Therefore, [the Buddha] calls out and addresses him, saying: "Śāriputra!"
Son, do not think that because I speak of emptiness you should then become attached to emptiness. As I have said, form is not different from emptiness;
as I have said, emptiness is not different from form. Yet, to merely say they are "not different" still implies two distinct things in relation to one another.
Even if they are joined as one, the notion of "one" still persists. In reality, what I speak of as form is precisely what I speak of as [emptiness].
Emptiness. There is no emptiness apart from form. What I call emptiness is precisely the teaching of form; there is no form apart from emptiness.
Not only is there no form, but there is also no emptiness. This is true emptiness. Therefore, he called out again and addressed him, saying:

Śāriputra, all these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness; there is not even emptiness that can be named, let alone further names and characteristics such as arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease.
Therefore, form is fundamentally unarisen, and emptiness is fundamentally undestroyed. One speaks of form as non-defiled and emptiness as non-pure.
It does not increase within form, nor does it decrease within emptiness. This is not because one conceals it; rather, from the very beginning, such things do not exist within emptiness.
Therefore, the five aggregates are all empty; there is no form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. The six sense faculties are all empty;
there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. The six sense objects are all empty; there is no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomenon. The eighteen elements are all empty;
there is no element of the eye, and so on, up to and including the element of mental consciousness. This extends even to birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as ignorance and...
Ignorance—wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths, realization, and so forth—are all unattainable.

In this way, the wisdom-observation of this sovereign Bodhisattva reaches the further shore of non-attainment. Since nothing is attained, there naturally arises no obstruction, fear, or inverted delusions.
While manifesting within birth and death, one ultimately realizes nirvana. How much more so...

Bodhisattvas, as well as all Buddhas of the three periods—past, present, and future—likewise attain the other shore by means of this wisdom and together realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus, one may truly believe that it applies to all sentient beings throughout the entire earth.

There is not one who is not a Buddha. Thus we know that this wondrous wisdom of true emptiness is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the peerless mantra.
It is capable of leading one out of the sea of suffering of birth and death and delivering all from their afflictions and calamities;
it is true and not false. Now, it has long been difficult to speak of emptiness. Those who cling to form...
The color of mud. Those who speak of emptiness become stuck in emptiness; yet when both [emptiness and form] have no basis, they then deny all causes and effects.
They do not believe the clear praise within the sutras that "emptiness is itself form"—what further emptiness could there be? And that "form is itself emptiness"—what further form could there be?
When there is neither emptiness nor form, what further existence or non-existence could there be to cause me any obstruction? And...

Is it not that one lacks self-mastery? However, as for the observer, if one simply uses the wisdom of one's own house to contemplate and illuminate constantly, then the other shore shall be attained spontaneously.
How could a Bodhisattva be anyone other than oneself? It is merely a matter of being able to perform this single act of contemplative illumination.
Every person is a Bodhisattva, yet they do not see themselves as such. Therefore, when one speaks of a Bodhisattva, every person is one with them.

There is no difference between the sage and the fool. When one speaks of the Buddhas of the three periods, they are one and the same across past and present; there is neither priority nor posteriority.
Yet, alas, how can it be that so many are made to follow [the path] but not made to know it? If they could be made to know, they would become Bodhisattvas;
if they cannot be made to know, they become common folk, or birds and beasts, or wood and stone, ultimately returning to a state of indistinct oblivion.
Outline of the Heart Sutra (End)
